sections.h2: Where Osceola County records are kept
sections.html:
Everything recordable in Osceola County lands at the same counter. The clerk of the circuit and county courts also serves as comptroller and county recorder, and the clerk's website, osceolaclerk.com, carries the recording forms, eRecording, tax deed information and the property fraud alert signup.

Documents go into one running series called the Official Records. Nothing leaves that series unless a court orders it. Parcel values and exemptions are a different matter: those belong to the Property Appraiser at 2505 E. Irlo Bronson Memorial Highway in Kissimmee.

The recording list is broad. It covers deeds, leases, mortgages, liens, judgments and other instruments that affect real or personal property.

  • Deeds, mortgages, notices or claims of lien, plus their releases and satisfactions
  • Lis pendens notices, which announce that a lawsuit touches a property
  • Judgments and their assignments, releases and satisfactions
  • Federal tax liens and the certificates releasing them
  • Certified death certificates and military discharge records

Sellers should pay attention to two entries in particular. A foreclosure case in progress appears as a lis pendens against the parcel. A recorded judgment can attach to any land the debtor owns.

A deed that misses the clerk's formal checklist can be returned until it is fixed. The clerk's page points to Florida Statute 695.26 and spells out what the face of the document must show.

  • The grantor's notarized signature, with a printed name and address beneath it
  • Two witnesses with printed names; on documents dated January 1, 2024 or later, their post office addresses too
  • A full legal description
  • The grantee's mailing address, along with the preparer's name and address, written as a person's first and last name and not only a business name
  • A blank 3 by 3 inch area in the top right corner, reserved for the clerk
  • Original ink signatures, because photocopies are refused

The office does not run title searches. It sends people who need one to a title agency or an attorney.

Expect $10.00 for the first page and $8.50 for each page after that. Deed stamps are added at $0.70 per $100.

Charges in the clerk's recording FAQ

Recording, first page$10.00

A deed showing only token consideration still owes the minimum stamp of $0.70.

Bring a business check, cashier's check, money order or cash. Personal checks are turned away. Credit and debit cards work only at the counter, with a 3.5 percent surcharge.

The Recording Department sits upstairs at the courthouse, 2 Courthouse Square, Kissimmee, FL 34741. The building stays open through the afternoon on weekdays, but the recording window shuts at 4:30 p.m. A deed handed in after that is recorded the next business day. The recording line is (407) 742-3517, and the main clerk line is 407-742-3500. Anyone mailing a deed should include a self-addressed, postage-paid return envelope. The clerk also accepts e-recordings.

sections.h2: Searching Official Records and ordering copies
sections.html:
The online Official Records search runs around the clock. For paper, you can buy copies in person, electronically, or through PERCH Search or MyFloridaCounty at $1.00 per page. Each certification adds $2.00, and plat copies cost $5.00 per page.

The cheapest protection available is the clerk's Property Fraud Alert. The office has no way to verify who actually signed a paper placed in front of it, and only a judge can order a bad filing removed. An alert that tells you when something is recorded under your name gives you an early warning while the house is being prepared for sale.

sections.h2: If a bad document appears on your property
sections.html:
Report it quickly. The clerk cannot pull a filing without a court order. Depending on where the home sits, the clerk's FAQ suggests the Kissimmee Police Department, the St. Cloud Police Department or the Osceola County Sheriff's Office, and says a document touching several Florida locations may go to the Florida Department of Law Enforcement.

Section 817.535 of the Florida Statutes makes recording a fraudulent instrument against property a third degree felony, and a court can order such a document voided and removed. Tell your title agent the moment you find an odd entry. A buyer's lender will not close over a lien or deed nobody can explain.

Real estate tax left unpaid in Osceola turns delinquent at the start of April and picks up a 3 percent addition. The collector auctions certificates on those parcels online by June 1, with bids opening at 18 percent and falling from there.

The clerk runs tax deed sales online. A certificate that sits untouched can support a tax deed application from April 1 of the second year after it was bought. If the winning bidder backs out, the deposit is forfeited; it is the greater of 5 percent of the bid or $200, and the balance is due within a day. Tax deed land sells as is, and the clerk warns that no promise of clear title comes with it.

When a sale produces overbid money, the claim is an affidavit sent to the clerk's Tax Deed Department.

sections.h2: Dates on the Osceola tax bill
sections.html:
The Tax Collector's calendar rests on a handful of fixed dates. Payments open in November at a 4 percent discount, step down to 3, 2 and 1 percent through February, and reach the full amount in March.

Requests to join the quarterly installment plan are due by April 30. Installments then fall on June 30, September 30 and December 31. An installment that misses July 31 loses its discount, adds a 5 percent penalty and ends the plan.

  • April 1: delinquent, with 3 percent added to the gross amount
  • Three weeks of newspaper advertising before the certificate sale
  • On or before June 1: online tax certificate sale
  • Redeeming on or after June 1 adds a $6.25 fee

Interest on a sold certificate follows the rate at which it sold, so get the payoff in writing for your own closing day.

sections.h2: Steps before a sale, in order
sections.html:
Search the Official Records under your name and the property description. Read each hit against your deed. Look for any mortgage that was paid but never released, any lien or judgment, and any lis pendens. Fix paperwork gaps first, because a title company will find them anyway and each one can hold up a closing.

Next, check the tax account and ask the collector for a written payoff if anything is open. After closing, confirm the new deed was recorded and keep a stamped copy. If you are comparing a standard listing with a cash sale, these same steps apply to both. A cash sale mainly skips the lender's appraisal and underwriting, not the title work.

faqs.q: Which office records deeds in Osceola County?
faqs.a: The Osceola County Clerk of the Circuit Court and County Comptroller, acting as county recorder. The office is at 2 Courthouse Square in Kissimmee and records deeds, mortgages, liens and judgments.

faqs.q: What does it cost to record a one-page deed in Osceola County?
faqs.a: The clerk charges $10.00 for the first page, plus documentary stamp tax of $0.70 per $100 of consideration. Each added page costs $8.50, and names beyond four cost $1.00 each for indexing.

faqs.q: Can I pay with a personal check at the Osceola recording counter?
faqs.a: No. The clerk takes business checks, cashier's checks, money orders and cash, and credit cards in person with a 3.5 percent fee.

faqs.q: What time must I submit a deed in Osceola County?
faqs.a: Before 4:30 p.m. on a business day. The courthouse stays open until 5:00 p.m., but recording stops at 4:30, and later documents are recorded the next business day.

faqs.q: Can the clerk remove a fraudulent deed from the records?
faqs.a: Not on its own. The clerk can remove a recorded item only under a court order. Report suspected fraud to law enforcement, and consider the free Property Fraud Alert.
